rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3, two-year (2004-2005) field trial in a Cabernet Sauvignon vineyard in Sicily with three randomized blocks comparing surface drip (DR) and two subsurface drip placements (SDI 0, SDI 120). Q2: Section 3.6 and Table 5, yield per vine was higher under SDI 120 than DR (44% in 2004, 49.7% in 2005), SDI 0 intermediate and not significantly different from DR; Discussion/Conclusions state subsurface systems increased yield with 20% less water. Q4: Section 3.3 and Fig. 1, predawn leaf water potential measured before and after irrigations showing SDI vines reached similar water status with 20% less water; Sections 3.5 and Tables 4, 6, 8, root contacts/distribution and dry-mass partitioning measured and used to explain yield response. Q9: Table 5 reports yield, cluster and berry weight as means <U+00B1> standard errors per treatment and year.
rows.notes: The study supports the claim only as one data point (SDI increased yield relative to surface drip in this trial); the 'controversy' is the review's synthesis across studies. Yield measured by a single method (harvest weighing) so no triangulation. Single site, soil and cultivar; plot-level only. Authors note yield gain was significant only with the inter-row (SDI 120) line and that SDI 120 under deficit irrigation in sandy soil may harm reserve storage, but these are stated as observations/possible shortcomings rather than explicit requirements or limitations of the yield result; 'further investigation' statements are generic. Q4 answered yes on the basis of measured plant water status and root distribution; some doubt whether these count as the intermediate variable for yield.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study compares surface drip vs subsurface drip at two line positions under regulated deficit irrigation; subsurface treatments received 20% less water by design.
